children.value: Chapters 6 and 8 ended on the same observation: the dual form of ridge regression and the dual form of the support vector machine use the training examples only through their inner products. This chapter follows that observation to its conclusion. If we can compute the inner product of two feature vectors without ever building them, the feature space can be enormous, or even infinite-dimensional, and the cost of the method does not depend on its dimension. We shall characterize the functions that are inner products (the positive semidefinite kernels), prove the representer theorem, which says that the solution of a very large class of penalized problems is a combination of kernel functions centered at the training points, derive kernel ridge regression, use the SVM of Chapter 8 with the Gaussian kernel, and see how to approximate a kernel method when

children.value: The first half of the proof shows what is going on:
a Gram matrix is a matrix of inner products, and inner products make positive semidefinite matrices
. It also gives a practical test:
a function is not a kernel as soon as one Gram matrix has a negative eigenvalue

. The test can only refute (it cannot prove that a function is a kernel, which needs the algebra of the next section), but it is a useful sanity check for a kernel that we have made up. def loo_grid(K, yc, lams):
    """Leave-one-out RMSE of kernel ridge regression for many lambdas from one eigendecomposition (Proposition 9.6)."""
    mu, U = np.linalg.eigh(K)
    uy = U.T @ yc
    out = []
    for lam in lams:
        shrink = mu / (mu + lam)
        resid = yc - U @ (shrink * uy)
        h = (U**2) @ shrink
        out.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((resid / (1 - h)) ** 2)))
    return np.array(out)

def smo(K, y, C, tol=1e-8, max_iter=500_000):
    """Sequential minimal optimization (maximal violating pair) for the SVM dual with a Gram matrix K, labels in {-1, +1} (Section 8.5.2)."""
    n = len(y)
    alpha, G = np.zeros(n), -np.ones(n)
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        e = -y * G
        up = ((y == 1) & (alpha < C)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha > 0))
        low = ((y == 1) & (alpha > 0)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha < C))
        i = np.flatnonzero(up)[np.argmax(e[up])]
        j = np.flatnonzero(low)[np.argmin(e[low])]
        gap = e[i] - e[j]
        if gap <= tol:
            break
        a = max(K[i, i] + K[j, j] - 2 * K[i, j], 1e-12)
        t_i = (C - alpha[i]) if y[i] == 1 else alpha[i]
        t_j = alpha[j] if y[j] == 1 else (C - alpha[j])
        t = min(gap / a, t_i, t_j)
        d_i, d_j = y[i] * t, -y[j] * t
        alpha[i] += d_i
        alpha[j] += d_j
        G += (y * y[i]) * K[:, i] * d_i + (y * y[j]) * K[:, j] * d_j
    e = -y * G
    free = (alpha > 1e-10) & (alpha < C - 1e-10)
    if free.any():

def random_fourier_features(X, gamma, D, seed):
    """z(x) = sqrt(2/D) cos(W'x + b), W ~ N(0, 2 gamma I), b ~ U[0, 2 pi]  (Theorem 9.7)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

    b = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, size=D)
    return np.sqrt(2.0 / D) * np.cos(X @ W + b)
